newsitem.title: UK: Moody's says Pakistan banks face uphill climb.
newsitem.headline: Moody's says Pakistan banks face uphill climb.

text.p: Moody's rating agency said on Monday that Pakistan's banking sector faced a tough period while the current transition in the industry took place.
"The Pakistani banking industry is in the middle of a transition that will eventually make for stronger, more efficient and customer-oriented institutions," it said in a report.

But the report added that "the next several years will be crucial in sustaining the transition's momentum and that intensifying political tensions and regional instability may well take it off track."
The cornerstone of the changes was the privatisation of the largest commercial banks, the agency said. Two are already in private hands, while two more are scheduled to follow suit.

"The main political parties believe that the privatization program currently underway will improve management practices and bring about more responsible lending," it said, adding that is viewed both changes as long overdue.
Moody's currently rates four of the commercial banks in Pakistan: Habib Bank, United Bank, National Bank of Pakistan, and Muslim Commercial Bank.
The deposit ratings are set at Pakistan's sovereign ceilings of B3/Not Prime, and all four have very weak financial strength.
The report said that "decades of directed lending have resulted in deteriorating loan portfolios at Pakistan's main banks."
"The danger that this deterioration represents is compounded by the country's low household savings rate and by its political instability."
It adde that central bank supervision was falling behind the challenges of modern banking despite a marked improvement in recent years.
Moody said that the legal system, the judiciary, and the law enforcement agencies were ineffective, and that the procedures were slow and cumbersome.

"Additionally, Islamic banking principles have not been fully implemented, and there are grey areas in the usage of "proper" Islamic instruments and confusion over obligations arising out of transactions entered into before the "Islamisation" of banking in 1985," it said.
